warmup.q: The quote service answers within 300 ms. Northbank takes 10 calls at a time and needs 50 ms per call. A burst of 500 requests arrives at once, and the service queues them all. About how many get a live Northbank price?
options: All 500, each a little later than usual
About 50 to 60: ten at a time, and six rounds of 50 ms fit in 300 ms
None: the burst knocks Northbank over
warmup.why: Little's law: 10 calls at once at 50 ms each is at most 200 calls a second, so 300 ms holds about 60. This lesson's demo got 50, because the sixth round ends exactly at the deadline. The other 450 wait for a permit until their deadline and then fail. Queueing them didn't get them a price; it made them slow failures. Section 4 turns them into fast ones.

sections.h: A bulkhead for each provider, sized by Little's law
sections.html:
Lesson 2's fan-out sends every request to every provider at once. With a thousand requests in flight, Northbank sees a thousand concurrent calls, and its contract allows 10. Past that it answers 429, or slows down for everyone. The fix is a bulkhead: a limit on the calls in flight to one provider, so that one provider's limit doesn't become everybody's outage. In coroutines it is a Semaphore from kotlinx.coroutines.sync, the same tool "Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores" used from the JDK:

Java
// Java equivalent on virtual threads: java.util.concurrent.Semaphore, acquire before the try
private Quote once(String symbol) throws IOException, InterruptedException {
    permits.acquire();                                             // blocks a cheap virtual thread
    try {
        return delegate.quote(symbol);
    } finally {
        permits.release();
    }
}
Kotlin
class GuardedProvider(private val delegate: Provider, maxConcurrent: Int /* ... */) : Provider {
    private val permits = Semaphore(maxConcurrent)                 // kotlinx.coroutines.sync

    private suspend fun once(symbol: String): Quote =
        permits.withPermit { delegate.quote(symbol) }              // suspends while all permits are out
}

withPermit suspends while no permit is free. It holds no thread, and the wait is cancellable, so lesson 2's deadline still applies: a call that waits too long for a permit is cancelled with the rest and counts as no answer.

How many permits? Little's law ("Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law") says calls in flight equal arrival rate times time per call. If Northbank allows 10 calls at once and answers in 50 ms, it serves at most 200 calls a second. More permits add no capacity; they move the queue to Northbank's side, where you can't see it. Take the number from the provider's contract, and give each provider its own: Eastgate may allow 40, as the figure shows.

Two placement rules matter. The permit goes around each single call, not around a whole retry loop: a call that waits out its backoff shouldn't hold a permit, and a hedge is a second call that needs one of its own. And the bulkhead lives in the provider's wrapper, not around the fan-out. A limit on requests can't protect a provider, because each request makes three calls.

try.title: Forty requests, one provider, two limits
steps: Open BulkheadDemo.kt (virtual time) or BulkheadDemoJava.java (virtual threads, real time). Forty requests call a provider that answers in 50 ms.
Predict the most calls in flight at once, and the time until all forty are answered, with no limit and with a limit of 4.
Run it. Then change the limit to 8 and predict again from Little's law.

code.title: BulkheadDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.quotes.l03 import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.withPermit import kotlinx.coroutines.test.currentTime import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest /** 40 requests at once to a provider that answers in 50 ms. How many calls does it see at once? */ fun main() = runTest { // virtual time, one thread: plain counters are safe here for (limit in listOf(null, 4)) { val permits = limit?.let { Semaphore(it) } var active = 0 var peak = 0 suspend fun call() { active++ peak = maxOf(peak, active) delay(50) // the provider thinks active-- } val t0 = currentTime coroutineScope { repeat(40) { launch { if (permits == null) call() else permits.withPermit { call() } } } } println("%-9s calls in flight at most: %2d all 40 answered after %3d ms".format( if (limit == null) "no limit" else "limit $limit", peak, currentTime - t0)) } }

alt.title: BulkheadDemoJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent with virtual threads: one per request, and a java.util.concurrent.Semaphore as the bulkhead package workbench.quotes.l03; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** 40 requests at once to a provider that answers in 50 ms. How many calls does it see at once? Real time. */ public class BulkheadDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { for (Integer limit : new Integer[] {null, 4}) { Semaphore permits = limit == null ? null : new Semaphore(limit); AtomicInteger active = new AtomicInteger(); AtomicInteger peak = new AtomicInteger(); Runnable call = () -> { peak.accumulateAndGet(active.incrementAndGet(), Math::max); try { Thread.sleep(50); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } active.decrementAndGet(); }; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService vthreads = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (int i = 0; i < 40; i++) { vthreads.submit(() -> { if (permits == null) { call.run(); return null; } permits.acquire(); // acquire before the try try { call.run(); } finally { permits.release(); } return null; }); } } // close() waits for all 40 System.out.printf("%-9s calls in flight at most: %2d all 40 answered after %3d ms%n", limit == null ? "no limit" : "limit " + limit, peak.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } } }

try.expect: No limit: 40 calls at once, all answered after 50 ms. Limit 4: 4 at once, and 40 / 4 = 10 rounds of 50 ms, 500 ms. With a limit of 8 it is 5 rounds, 250 ms. The Java twin prints the same peaks in real time, with a few extra milliseconds of scheduling. The limit didn't make anything faster; it made the provider's load a number you chose.

sections.h: Retry only what is safe to repeat, and spread the retries
sections.html:
A transient failure, such as a 503 or a reset connection, often succeeds on a second try. But a retry is a second request, and the provider can't tell it from a new one. Northbank and Eastgate stream indicative prices, so asking twice changes nothing. Fjord's quotes are firm: each call reserves liquidity for two seconds and counts against our daily quota, and a retried firm quote reserves twice. So the decision belongs to the provider, as Provider.idempotent, false unless the provider says otherwise:

Java
// Java equivalent with Reactor: the same decision before any retry operator is added
Mono<Quote> quote(String symbol) {
    Mono<Quote> once = Mono.defer(() -> delegate.quote(symbol));
    if (!delegate.idempotent()) return once;                       // a firm quote: exactly one call
    return once.retryWhen(Retry.backoff(2, Duration.ofMillis(50)).jitter(0.5)
            .filter(e -> e instanceof IOException));
}
Kotlin
override suspend fun quote(symbol: String): Quote {
    val once: suspend () -> Quote = { permits.withPermit { delegate.quote(symbol) } }
    if (!delegate.idempotent) return once()                         // a firm quote: exactly one call
    val attempt: suspend () -> Quote = if (hedgeAfter == null) once else ({ hedged(hedgeAfter, once) })
    return retrying(backoff, random, attempt)
}

retrying is the backoff loop from "Shared state and testing coroutines" with one change, jitter. When Northbank blips, every request in flight fails in the same millisecond. Without jitter they all come back one backoff later, in the same millisecond again, and hit a provider that is still recovering. Multiplying each wait by a random factor between 0.5 and 1.5 spreads them out, which is what Reactor's Retry.backoff does by default ("Errors, retries and timeouts"):

Java
// Java equivalent on a virtual thread: the same factor, and a sleep that an interrupt ends
double factor = 1 + jitter * (ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextDouble() * 2 - 1);
Thread.sleep((long) (nominal(n).toMillis() * factor));
Kotlin
val factor = 1 + backoff.jitter * (random.nextDouble() * 2 - 1)   // 0.5 .. 1.5 for jitter 0.5
delay(backoff.nominal(n) * factor)                                  // cancellable: the deadline still rules

This section's demo has 1,000 clients that failed together and retry after a nominal 100 ms. Without jitter, all 1,000 retries land in one millisecond. With a jitter of 0.5 they spread over 50 to 150 ms, and no millisecond gets more than 18.

Three more rules keep retries honest. Retry only errors that a later attempt might fix: here an IOException, never an unknown symbol. Keep every wait cancellable, so the deadline cuts off retries that can't finish in time; a retry after the deadline is work nobody will read. And count the calls: two retries means up to three calls per request, and Little's law applies to those as well.

try.title: A thousand retries in one millisecond
steps: Open RetryJitterDemo.kt (or the Java twin, which computes the same waits without sleeping). A thousand clients failed together at 0 ms and retry after a nominal 100 ms.
Predict how the retries spread over 25 ms buckets with no jitter and with a jitter of 0.5, and the most retries in any single millisecond.
Run it. Then set the jitter to 0.1 and predict the busiest millisecond.

code.title: RetryJitterDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.quotes.l03 import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.test.currentTime import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest import kotlin.random.Random import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.milliseconds /** 1,000 clients fail together at 0 ms and retry after a nominal 100 ms. When do the retries land? */ fun main() = runTest { for (jitter in listOf(0.0, 0.5)) { val random = Random(7) val retryAt = IntArray(1_000) val t0 = currentTime coroutineScope { repeat(1_000) { client -> launch { val factor = 1 + jitter * (random.nextDouble() * 2 - 1) // 1 - jitter .. 1 + jitter delay(100.milliseconds * factor) retryAt[client] = (currentTime - t0).toInt() } } } val buckets = retryAt.groupBy { it / 25 * 25 }.toSortedMap() println("jitter $jitter: " + buckets.entries.joinToString(" ") { (from, hits) -> "$from-${from + 24} ms: ${hits.size}" }) println(" most retries in one millisecond: ${retryAt.groupBy { it }.values.maxOf { it.size }}") } }

alt.title: RetryJitterDemoJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent: the same jitter formula with java.util.Random; the waits are computed, not slept package workbench.quotes.l03; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Random; import java.util.TreeMap; /** 1,000 clients fail together at 0 ms and retry after a nominal 100 ms. When do the retries land? */ public class RetryJitterDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { for (double jitter : new double[] {0.0, 0.5}) { Random random = new Random(7); Map<Integer, Integer> buckets = new TreeMap<>(); Map<Integer, Integer> perMs = new TreeMap<>(); for (int client = 0; client < 1_000; client++) { double factor = 1 + jitter * (random.nextDouble() * 2 - 1); // 1 - jitter .. 1 + jitter int at = (int) Math.ceil(100 * factor); // delay rounds up to whole ms buckets.merge(at / 25 * 25, 1, Integer::sum); perMs.merge(at, 1, Integer::sum); } StringBuilder line = new StringBuilder("jitter " + jitter + ":"); buckets.forEach((from, hits) -> line.append(String.format(" %d-%d ms: %d", from, from + 24, hits))); System.out.println(line); System.out.println(" most retries in one millisecond: " + perMs.values().stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).max().orElse(0)); } } }

try.expect: No jitter: all 1,000 retries in the 100 to 124 ms bucket, and all of them in the same millisecond. Jitter 0.5: about 250 in each bucket from 50 to 149 ms (a few land at exactly 150 after rounding up), and the busiest millisecond has 18. With 0.1 the retries squeeze into 90 to 110 ms, and the busiest millisecond gets 58, three times as many: less jitter, less spread.

sections.h: Hedge the slow tail of one provider
sections.html:
Northbank answers in 40 ms most of the time, but one call in twenty takes 600 ms: a garbage-collection pause, or a slow replica. A retry doesn't help, because nothing failed; the call is just slow. A hedge does. If the first call hasn't answered by the time 95% of calls have, send one more identical call and take whichever answers first:

Java
// Java equivalent with Reactor: the delayed hedge is cancelled before it starts if the first call wins
Mono<Quote> hedged(Duration after, Mono<Quote> call) {
    return Mono.firstWithValue(call, Mono.delay(after).then(call));
}
Kotlin
suspend fun <T : Any> hedged(after: Duration, call: suspend () -> T): T = coroutineScope {
    val first = async { call() }
    val early = withTimeoutOrNull(after) { first.await() }    // stops the waiting, not the call
    if (early != null) return@coroutineScope early
    val second = async { call() }                              // the hedge
    val winner = select { first.onAwait { it }; second.onAwait { it } }
    coroutineContext.cancelChildren()                          // stop the loser
    winner
}

withTimeoutOrNull(after) { first.await() } stops waiting at the hedge time. It doesn't cancel first, which is a child of the coroutineScope, not of the timeout. Then select takes whichever deferred completes first ("Channels, select and pipelines"), and cancelChildren() stops the loser. Forget that line and coroutineScope waits for the slow call anyway, which undoes the hedge. In this section's demo, 200 Northbank quotes went from a p99 of 600 ms to a p99 of 120 ms, for 210 calls instead of 200. Hedging at the 95th percentile costs about 5% more calls.

That cost decides where hedges go. Hedge only an idempotent provider, because a hedge is a duplicate request. Hedge only the provider whose tail hurts, here Northbank, at a time taken from its measured latency. And make the hedge take its own permit from the bulkhead. When Northbank is saturated, a hedge would only add to the queue that made it slow, so under full load the hedge waits for a permit, and the first call usually wins. The lab has a test for exactly that: with one permit, the hedge never runs alongside the first call.

try.title: Cut Northbank's tail
steps: Open HedgeDemo.kt. Northbank answers in 40 ms, except every 20th call, which takes 600 ms. The demo asks for 200 quotes without a hedge, then with a hedge after 80 ms.
Predict p50, p99, the slowest request and the number of calls for both runs.
Run it. Then set the hedge to 30 ms, below Northbank's normal latency, and predict the number of calls.

code.title: HedgeDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.quotes.l03 import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.cancelChildren import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.selects.select import kotlinx.coroutines.test.currentTime import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeoutOrNull private var calls = 0 // Northbank: 40 ms, except every 20th call, which takes 600 ms (its slow 5%) private suspend fun northbank(): String { val n = ++calls delay(if (n % 20 == 0) 600 else 40) return "northbank 1.0845" } private suspend fun <T : Any> hedged(afterMs: Long, call: suspend () -> T): T = coroutineScope { val first = async { call() } val early = withTimeoutOrNull(afterMs) { first.await() } if (early != null) return@coroutineScope early val second = async { call() } // the hedge select { first.onAwait { it }; second.onAwait { it } }.also { coroutineContext.cancelChildren() } } /** 200 quotes from Northbank, one after another, with and without a hedge after 80 ms. */ fun main() = runTest { for (hedgeAfter in listOf(null, 80L)) { calls = 0 val latencies = (1..200).map { val t0 = currentTime if (hedgeAfter == null) northbank() else hedged(hedgeAfter) { northbank() } currentTime - t0 }.sorted() println("%-15s p50 %3d ms p99 %3d ms max %3d ms calls to Northbank: %d".format( if (hedgeAfter == null) "no hedge" else "hedge at $hedgeAfter ms", latencies[99], latencies[197], latencies.last(), calls)) } }

alt.title: HedgeDemoJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent with Reactor: Mono.firstWithValue races the call against a hedge that starts after 80 ms package workbench.quotes.l03; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** 200 quotes from Northbank, all at once, with and without a hedge after 80 ms. Real time. */ public class HedgeDemoJava { static final AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger(); // Northbank: 40 ms, except every 20th call, which takes 600 ms (its slow 5%) static Mono<String> northbank() { return Mono.defer(() -> { int n = calls.incrementAndGet(); return Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(n % 20 == 0 ? 600 : 40)).thenReturn("northbank 1.0845"); }); } static Mono<String> hedged(Duration after) { // the delayed hedge is cancelled before it starts if the first call answers in time return Mono.firstWithValue(northbank(), Mono.delay(after).then(northbank())); } public static void main(String[] args) { for (Duration hedgeAfter : new Duration[] {null, Duration.ofMillis(80)}) { calls.set(0); List<Long> latencies = Flux.range(1, 200) .flatMap(i -> { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); Mono<String> q = hedgeAfter == null ? northbank() : hedged(hedgeAfter); return q.map(x -> (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); }, 200) .sort() .collectList().block(); System.out.printf("%-15s p50 %3d ms p99 %3d ms max %3d ms calls to Northbank: %d%n", hedgeAfter == null ? "no hedge" : "hedge at 80 ms", latencies.get(99), latencies.get(197), latencies.get(199), calls.get()); } } }

try.expect: No hedge: p50 40 ms, p99 and max 600 ms, 200 calls. Hedge at 80 ms: p50 still 40, p99 and max 120 ms (80 ms of waiting plus a 40 ms hedge), 210 calls. With the hedge at 30 ms every request is hedged: 400 calls, twice the load, for a p99 that the 80 ms hedge already got down to 120. A hedge time below the normal latency duplicates every request. The Java twin uses Reactor's Mono.firstWithValue and prints about the same numbers in real time, give or take the scheduling delays of a busy machine.

sections.h: Shed load at the door, then shut down in order
sections.html:
Bulkheads protect the providers. Nothing yet protects the service from more requests than it can answer within its deadline. Northbank takes 10 calls at a time at 50 ms each, so within 300 ms it can answer about 60 requests, and a burst of 500 leaves hundreds waiting for a permit until they fail at the deadline anyway. This section's demo measured it: 50 live answers, 450 misses, and 135,000 ms of waiting (summed over the requests that missed) that produced nothing.

Load shedding turns those slow failures into fast ones. QuoteService admits at most maxInFlight requests, and the next one gets a failed future at once, which lesson 1's handler writes as 7 ERR busy:

Java
// Java equivalent: the same door with a java.util.concurrent.Semaphore
public CompletableFuture<Quote> quote(String symbol) {
    if (!accepting) return CompletableFuture.failedFuture(new ShuttingDownException());
    if (!admission.tryAcquire()) return CompletableFuture.failedFuture(new BusyException());
    CompletableFuture<Quote> reply = best(symbol).toFuture();
    reply.whenComplete((q, e) -> admission.release());
    return reply;
}
Kotlin
override fun quote(symbol: String): CompletableFuture<Quote> {
    if (!accepting) return CompletableFuture.failedFuture(ShuttingDownException())
    if (!admission.tryAcquire()) return CompletableFuture.failedFuture(BusyException())   // never waits
    val reply = scope.future { best.quote(symbol) }
    reply.whenComplete { _, _ -> admission.release() }         // however the request ends
    return reply
}

With 50 admitted, the same burst got the same 50 live answers, and the other 450 clients heard busy within a millisecond, early enough to try another instance. tryAcquire never waits, so the event loop that calls quote never waits either. The permit comes back in whenComplete, however the request ends, including a cancel after a hang-up.

Shutdown uses the same pieces, in the order "Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown" gave for thread pools:

Java
// Java equivalent for an executor-based service: the same order, from "Pools in production"
void shutdown(Duration grace) throws InterruptedException {
    server.stopAccepting();                                      // 1. no new connections
    accepting = false;                                           // 2. stop admitting
    pool.shutdown();
    if (!pool.awaitTermination(grace.toMillis(), MILLISECONDS)) {   // 3. drain, up to grace
        pool.shutdownNow();                                      // 4. interrupt the rest
        pool.awaitTermination(5, SECONDS);
    }
    server.close();                                              // 5. close connections, stop the loops
}
Kotlin
suspend fun shutdown(grace: Duration): Int {
    accepting = false                                            // 2. stop admitting
    val job = scope.coroutineContext.job
    withTimeoutOrNull(grace) { job.children.toList().joinAll() }   // 3. drain, up to grace
    val left = job.children.count()
    job.cancelAndJoin()                                          // 4. cancel the rest, wait for them
    return left
}

// QuoteApp: 1. server.stopAccepting(), then the above, then 5. server.close()

Stop accepting connections. Stop admitting requests (ERR shutting down). Give the requests in flight a grace period to finish. Cancel what is left and wait for it with cancelAndJoin(), so that no coroutine outlives the service. Then close the connections and the loops. Lesson 1's ChannelGroup matters here: each connection is closed on its own loop, behind the reply that the drain just let through.

try.title: Queue the burst, or shed it
steps: Open ShedDemo.kt. A burst of 500 requests meets a provider that takes 10 calls at a time, 50 ms each, under a 300 ms deadline.
Predict the live answers, the misses, the requests shed as busy, and the time spent waiting for nothing, for both runs.
Run it. Then admit 100 instead of 50 and predict the misses again.

code.title: ShedDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.quotes.l03 import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.withPermit import kotlinx.coroutines.test.currentTime import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeoutOrNull /** * A burst of 500 requests. The provider takes 10 calls at a time, 50 ms each, and every request * has a 300 ms deadline. Queue them all, or shed what can't make the deadline? */ fun main() = runTest { for (maxInFlight in listOf(null, 50)) { val provider = Semaphore(10) val admission = maxInFlight?.let { Semaphore(it) } var live = 0 var late = 0 var busy = 0 var waitedForNothing = 0L coroutineScope { repeat(500) { launch { if (admission != null && !admission.tryAcquire()) { busy++ // answered "ERR busy" at once return@launch } try { val start = currentTime val answer = withTimeoutOrNull(300) { provider.withPermit { delay(50) } } if (answer != null) live++ else { late++; waitedForNothing += currentTime - start } } finally { admission?.release() } } } } println("%-14s live answers: %3d missed the deadline: %3d shed as busy: %3d ms spent waiting for nothing: %,d".format( if (maxInFlight == null) "queue them all" else "admit $maxInFlight", live, late, busy, waitedForNothing)) } }

alt.html: // Java equivalent with virtual threads: Semaphore.tryAcquire() sheds, a timed tryAcquire is the deadline package workbench.quotes.l03; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; /** * A burst of 500 requests. The provider takes 10 calls at a time, 50 ms each, and every request * has a 300 ms deadline. Queue them all, or shed what can't make the deadline? Real time. */ public class ShedDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { for (Integer maxInFlight : new Integer[] {null, 50}) { Semaphore provider = new Semaphore(10); Semaphore admission = maxInFlight == null ? null : new Semaphore(maxInFlight); AtomicInteger live = new AtomicInteger(), late = new AtomicInteger(), busy = new AtomicInteger(); AtomicLong waitedForNothing = new AtomicLong(); try (ExecutorService vthreads = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (int i = 0; i < 500; i++) { vthreads.submit(() -> { if (admission != null && !admission.tryAcquire()) { busy.incrementAndGet(); return null; } // ERR busy long start = System.nanoTime(); try { long deadline = start + TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.toNanos(300); if (provider.tryAcquire(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { try { Thread.sleep(50); } finally { provider.release(); } if (System.nanoTime() <= deadline) { live.incrementAndGet(); return null; } } late.incrementAndGet(); waitedForNothing.addAndGet((System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000); } finally { if (admission != null) admission.release(); } return null; }); } } System.out.printf("%-14s live answers: %3d missed the deadline: %3d shed as busy: %3d ms spent waiting for nothing: %,d%n", maxInFlight == null ? "queue them all" : "admit " + maxInFlight, live.get(), late.get(), busy.get(), waitedForNothing.get()); } } }

try.expect: Queue them all: 50 live answers, 450 misses, and 135,000 ms spent waiting by requests that got nothing. Admit 50: the same 50 live answers, 0 misses, 450 shed at once, and no wasted waiting. Admitting 100 gives the same 50 live answers, 50 misses and 15,000 ms of wasted waiting: past what the provider can serve in 300 ms, a bigger door only buys slow failures. The Java twin does the same with virtual threads in real time, so on a busy machine its numbers can drift by a few requests.

refs.title: cancelAndJoin (kotlinx.coroutines API, from the Job documentation)

sections.h: Design review: would one virtual thread per connection be simpler?
sections.html:
Here is the finished design next to the question every reviewer asks about it: wouldn't one virtual thread per connection, with plain blocking calls, be simpler?

Concern This service One virtual thread per connection
idle connections a few loop threads hold thousands one parked virtual thread each, a few KB
waiting for providers suspended coroutines blocked virtual threads
deadline and cancel structured: the cancel reaches every provider call interrupts, which some blocking clients ignore
per-provider limits a Semaphore per provider a Semaphore per provider
framing and backpressure Netty codecs, auto-read your own read loop; TCP does the pacing
code shape futures at the Java edge, coroutines inside plain blocking Java

Virtual threads ("The thread-per-request wall") make the right column cheap, and for many services they are the better choice. Switch when the providers only ship blocking SDKs, such as JDBC or an old SOAP client: this design would then need a blocking pool behind the coroutines, and you'd pay for two models. Switch when the team writes Java and connections number in the thousands. Stay on the event loop when the service already lives on Netty (Vert.x, Quarkus), when connections number in the hundreds of thousands, when you need the protocol control that auto-read and codecs give you, or when the provider clients are non-blocking and a cancel must reach them.

Either way, the limits stay. Bulkheads, deadlines, admission and an ordered shutdown appear in both columns, because moving to virtual threads removes the pool, and with it the only limit nobody wrote down ("Moving a blocking service to virtual threads"). The question that picks the model is where the waiting happens ("Zero-copy, epoll, io_uring, and choosing a server model"). Here it happens in three provider calls per request, under a deadline, and both models can wait well.

analogy: Picture the quote service as a restaurant on a Friday night with three suppliers. Each supplier has its own loading dock with a fixed number of bays: a truck that arrives when the bays are full waits outside (a bulkhead per provider). The host at the front door stops seating guests the kitchen can't serve before the theatre starts, and says so at once instead of letting them stand for an hour (shedding with ERR busy). A plate that comes out wrong is made again, but only when remaking is harmless; nobody runs the card twice (retry only idempotent calls). When one cook is slow, a second cook starts the same dish and the first plate out goes to the table (a hedge). At closing time the doors lock, the guests already eating finish, and the kitchen shuts after the last plate (an ordered shutdown). The analogy breaks at the hedge: a restaurant bins the second plate and eats the cost, while a provider counts both calls against your limit, which is why you hedge only the slow 5%.
world: The same guards sit in front of every payments dependency, with one difference that matters more than all the others: most payment calls are not idempotent. A card authorization, a capture or a refund must never be retried or hedged blindly, because the issuer can't tell a repeat from a new charge. Retry it only with the same idempotency key, and when the retries run out, mark it pending and reconcile, as "Errors, retries and timeouts" said. Reads are different: a balance, an FX rate or a BIN lookup can take a retry and a hedge. Give each issuer or acquirer its own bulkhead from its published limit, and pick one layer to own retries: a Temporal activity retry policy, SmallRye Fault Tolerance @Retry and a hand-written loop stacked on top of each other multiply the calls. During a Kubernetes rollout, the same shutdown order applies: fail the readiness check first so no new traffic arrives, drain within the termination grace period, then exit.
mistake: The most common load mistake is one retry policy for everything: every provider call, firm quotes and authorizations included, wrapped in the same retry(3) with no jitter. Under a short outage it sends synchronized waves of calls at a provider that is trying to recover, and for calls that aren't idempotent it does the work two or three times. The runner-up is an unbounded queue in front of a bounded resource: no admission limit, so a burst turns into hundreds of requests waiting for a permit until each one fails at its deadline, while the latency graph says the service is slow rather than full. Retry only idempotent calls, with jitter, inside the deadline, and shed at the door what you can't answer in time.

compare.title: The guards around a provider with coroutines and on virtual threads

java.title: GuardedProvider.java (virtual threads)
java.html: // Java on virtual threads: the same guards around a blocking provider client final class GuardedProvider { private final BlockingProvider delegate; private final Semaphore permits; private final Backoff backoff; GuardedProvider(BlockingProvider delegate, int maxConcurrent, Backoff backoff) { this.delegate = delegate; this.permits = new Semaphore(maxConcurrent); this.backoff = backoff; } Quote quote(String symbol) throws IOException, InterruptedException { if (!delegate.idempotent()) return once(symbol); // 2. never repeat a firm quote for (int n = 1; ; n++) { try { return once(symbol); } catch (IOException e) { if (n > backoff.retries()) throw e; // out of retries double factor = 1 + backoff.jitter() * (ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextDouble() * 2 - 1); Thread.sleep((long) (backoff.nominal(n).toMillis() * factor)); // an interrupt ends it } } } private Quote once(String symbol) throws IOException, InterruptedException { permits.acquire(); // 1. every call holds a permit try { return delegate.quote(symbol); } finally { permits.release(); } } }

kotlin.title: Resilience.kt
kotlin.html: suspend fun <T> retrying(backoff: Backoff, random: Random, call: suspend () -> T): T { var n = 0 while (true) { try { return call() } catch (e: IOException) { if (++n > backoff.retries) throw e // out of retries val factor = 1 + backoff.jitter * (random.nextDouble() * 2 - 1) // 1 - jitter .. 1 + jitter delay(backoff.nominal(n) * factor) // so callers that failed together spread out } } } class GuardedProvider( private val delegate: Provider, maxConcurrent: Int, private val backoff: Backoff = Backoff(), private val hedgeAfter: Duration? = null, private val random: Random = Random.Default, ) : Provider { private val permits = Semaphore(maxConcurrent) override val name: String get() = delegate.name override val idempotent: Boolean get() = delegate.idempotent override suspend fun quote(symbol: String): Quote { val once: suspend () -> Quote = { permits.withPermit { delegate.quote(symbol) } } // 1. every call holds a permit if (!delegate.idempotent) return once() // 2. never repeat a firm quote val attempt: suspend () -> Quote = if (hedgeAfter == null) once else ({ hedged(hedgeAfter, once) }) return retrying(backoff, random, attempt) // 3. a hedge per attempt } }

compare.note: The rules are the same in both: a permit around every single call, one call for a provider that isn't idempotent, and jittered retries for IOException only. What differs is what waiting and stopping cost. In Kotlin, withPermit and delay suspend, so a thousand requests waiting for a permit or a backoff hold no threads, and a cancel (the deadline or a hang-up) reaches them at once through the job tree. On virtual threads, acquire and Thread.sleep block, which is cheap too, and a cancel is an interrupt: it reaches the sleep and the semaphore, but only reaches the provider call if its client responds to interrupts. The Java version leaves the hedge out. On threads a hedge takes an ExecutorCompletionService, or JDK 25's StructuredTaskScope, still a preview API ("Structured concurrency and scoped values"), and the loser is stopped by an interrupt, which works only if its client responds to interrupts. Java code that can block on a virtual thread is shorter to read. Kotlin code gets the hedge and the deadline from the library.

worked.title: Trace one request through every guard on a bad afternoon

steps.say: The scene: 49 requests are in flight (the limit is 50), Northbank's next call is one of its slow ones, and Eastgate is returning a 503 now and then. A request for EURUSD arrives. It takes the last admission permit, so the next request will hear ERR busy.
steps.code: override fun quote(symbol: String): CompletableFuture<Quote> { if (!admission.tryAcquire()) return CompletableFuture.failedFuture(BusyException()) // 49 -> 50: admitted val reply = scope.future { best.quote(symbol) } // 300 ms deadline per provider call reply.whenComplete { _, _ -> admission.release() } return reply }

alt.html: // Java equivalent: the same admission check in front of a Reactor fan-out if (!admission.tryAcquire()) return CompletableFuture.failedFuture(new BusyException()); // 49 -> 50: admitted CompletableFuture<Quote> reply = best(symbol).toFuture(); // 300 ms deadline per provider call reply.whenComplete((q, e) -> admission.release()); return reply;

steps.say: BestQuote starts the three provider calls at 0 ms, each under the 300 ms deadline. Northbank's first call is slow, so at 80 ms the hedge starts with a second permit. Fjord's quote is firm, so it gets exactly one call and no hedge.
steps.code:
0 ms  northbank  permit 1 of 10, call 1 starts
 80 ms  northbank  no answer yet: the hedge takes permit 2 of 10, call 2 starts
120 ms  northbank  call 2 answers 1.0845; call 1 is cancelled, both permits are back
  0 ms  fjord      permit 1 of 5, one firm call (never retried, never hedged)
200 ms  fjord      answers 1.0843

steps.say: Eastgate fails at 30 ms with an IOException. Its permit goes back during the backoff, and the jittered wait (65 ms here) puts the retry at 95 ms. By 200 ms every provider has answered, so BestQuote doesn't need the deadline at all this time.
steps.code:
0 ms  eastgate   permit, call 1
 30 ms  eastgate   IOException: 503; permit back; wait 50 ms x 1.3 = 65 ms
 95 ms  eastgate   permit, call 2
145 ms  eastgate   answers 1.0841
200 ms  BestQuote  all three answered: eastgate 1.0841 wins; admission permit back (50 -> 49)

steps.say: Self-check: run the same afternoon, but the client hangs up at 100 ms. Which calls are running at that moment, what stops them, and when does the admission count drop back to 49? (Four calls are running: Northbank's slow first call and its hedge, Eastgate's retry and Fjord's firm call. Lesson 1's channelInactive cancels the future, scope.future cancels the request coroutine, and the cancel reaches all four, the hedge included. The future completes at once, so whenComplete releases the admission permit at 100 ms.)

lab.title: Bulkheads, retries, a hedge, shedding and shutdown
steps: Run the tests. All 13 fail. The l03 package already holds lessons 1 and 2's solutions; Provider now has idempotent, and QuoteApp.kt wires the server, the service and the shutdown order.

Write GuardedProvider.quote (points 1 to 3 of its KDoc): a Semaphore field, a permit around every single call, one call for a provider that isn't idempotent, retrying for the rest, and hedged around each attempt when hedgeAfter is set.
Add the jitter to retrying: one line that computes the factor, and the delay that uses it.
Write hedged as its KDoc describes. The bulkhead, retry and hedge tests should pass now.
In QuoteService, add the admission Semaphore and the accepting flag to quote, then write shutdown. Run the tests until all 13 pass, including the two over TCP, then run them twice more.
hints: If the bulkhead test sees more than 4 calls at once, the permit isn't around every call. If the limit counts hedges too sees 2, the hedge runs outside the permit: wrap the permit inside the function you pass to hedged.

select { first.onAwait { it }; second.onAwait { it } } is in kotlinx.coroutines.selects. Without coroutineContext.cancelChildren() after it, coroutineScope waits for the slow call and the hedge test reads 1,000 ms instead of 130.
Semaphore.tryAcquire() never suspends, so quote can call it on the event loop. Release in whenComplete on the returned future, so a request that is cancelled gives its permit back too.
In shutdown, join a snapshot of the children inside withTimeoutOrNull(grace), count what is still running, then cancelAndJoin() the scope's job.
lab.done: All 13 tests in UnderLoadTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Write the hedge from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write suspend fun <T : Any> hedged(after: Duration, call: suspend () -> T): T: start the call, and if it hasn't answered after after, start one more, return the first answer and stop the other. Which line, if you leave it out, makes the hedge useless, and why?

answer.html: suspend fun <T : Any> hedged(after: Duration, call: suspend () -> T): T = coroutineScope { val first = async { call() } val early = withTimeoutOrNull(after) { first.await() } // stop waiting, not the call if (early != null) return@coroutineScope early val second = async { call() } val winner = select { first.onAwait { it }; second.onAwait { it } } coroutineContext.cancelChildren() // or coroutineScope waits for the loser winner }

alt.html: // Java equivalent with Reactor <T> Mono<T> hedged(Duration after, Mono<T> call) { return Mono.firstWithValue(call, Mono.delay(after).then(call)); // the loser is cancelled }

recap: Give each provider its own bulkhead, a Semaphore sized from its contract by Little's law, with a permit around every single call, hedges included.
Retry only idempotent calls, only errors a later attempt can fix, with jitter and inside the deadline. A firm quote, like an authorization, is called once.
Hedge the provider whose tail hurts, after about its p95 latency, and cancel the loser. In the demo p99 fell from 600 to 120 ms for 5% more calls.
Shed at the door with tryAcquire: a request that can't make the deadline gets ERR busy in a millisecond instead of failing after 300 ms in a queue.
Shut down in order: stop accepting, stop admitting, drain within a grace period, cancelAndJoin the rest, then close connections and loops. No coroutine outlives the service.

Event loop or virtual threads, the limits stay. Switch to virtual threads when the provider clients only block or the team writes plain Java; keep the event loop for huge connection counts, protocol control and non-blocking clients.

explain.prompt: Design review. A sceptical reviewer says: "This is too much machinery: Netty, coroutines, futures, semaphores, hedges. One virtual thread per connection with blocking provider clients would be simpler, and Netty buffers everything anyway." Defend your design: say what each guard protects against, what you would keep if you did switch to virtual threads, and when you would switch.
explain.answer: Each piece answers a failure we can name. The event loop never waits, and auto-read with a cap of 16 per connection keeps one greedy client from filling our memory, because Netty's buffers have no limit of their own. The fan-out asks three providers under one deadline in a supervisor scope, so a failed or slow provider just drops out, and a stale cached price beats no answer. Cancelling the future on hang-up cancels every provider call through the job tree. Under load, each provider gets a bulkhead sized from its contract, so we never send Northbank more than its 10 calls; only idempotent providers are retried, with jitter so recoveries aren't hit by synchronized waves, and Fjord's firm quotes are called once. Northbank's slow tail gets a hedge after its p95, which cut p99 from 600 to 120 ms for 5% more calls. Admission sheds what we can't answer in 300 ms with an immediate ERR busy instead of a slow failure, and shutdown stops intake, drains, cancels and joins the rest, and then closes, so nothing leaks. If we switched to virtual threads I'd keep every limit: the bulkheads, the deadline, admission and the shutdown order, because virtual threads remove the pool and with it the only limit we never wrote down. I'd switch if the providers only had blocking SDKs, because then this design needs a blocking pool anyway, or if the team prefers plain Java and connections stay in the thousands. I'd stay on Netty for huge connection counts, for the protocol control, or when the provider clients are non-blocking and cancellation has to reach them.

deeper.html:
What a production version of this service would add, roughly in the order it would hurt to miss them.

Metrics. Per provider: latency histograms (the hedge time comes from the p95), permits in use, calls retried, hedges sent and won, errors by type. Per service: requests admitted, shed and served stale, and the age of stale quotes. Without them, every number in this track (the 10 permits, the 80 ms hedge, the 50 in flight) is a guess.

A circuit breaker. Retries help with blips; they make a dead provider worse. A breaker counts recent failures and, past a threshold, stops calling the provider for a while, then lets a few trial calls through. It sits outside the retry loop, so an open breaker fails fast instead of retrying.

A retry budget. Cap retries as a share of all calls, for example 10%. During a long outage the budget runs out and the service stops multiplying its own load.

Adaptive limits. Fixed permits are right only for the load they were measured under. Adaptive concurrency limits change the permits from observed latency, the way TCP's congestion control finds a window: when latency rises, the limit shrinks before the provider falls over.

Deadline propagation and context. Send the time left with each provider call so that the provider can give up too, and carry the trace and request ids across the Netty-to-coroutine edge (asContextElement or MDCContext, as "Dispatchers and the coroutine context" showed), so that a slow quote can be found in the logs.

Fair admission. One heavy client can still take most of the 50 slots. Per-client quotas at the door, on top of the global limit, keep a single caller from crowding out the rest.

An operations story for shutdown. Fail the readiness check before the drain starts, so that the load balancer stops sending, and keep the grace period shorter than the platform's termination grace, or the platform kills the process mid-drain.
